summary: WISE 0855-0714 is a known brown dwarf, the coldest one catalogued, about 7.3 light-years away. WANDERERS compared its 2010 position with SPHEREx images from 2025 and 2026. It found the dwarf had moved 131 arcseconds, or 8.27 arcseconds per year, within 1.5% of the published 8.15. It is also 5.1 times brighter near 4 to 4.75 microns than at 3.3 microns, where methane absorbs light. That dip marks a cold, methane-rich atmosphere. Confidence is high, but Gaia can't see it, and 41 of 160 spectrum points are flagged.

qa.q: Why do we think this is what the card says?
qa.a: Two clues agree. It moved 131 arcseconds between 2010 and 2026, about 8.27 arcseconds per year. That is within 1.5% of the catalogued 8.15, and only very nearby objects move that fast across the sky. It is also 5.1 times brighter at 4 to 4.75 microns than in the 3.3 micron methane band, which is the methane dip of a cold brown dwarf. Gaia can't see it, and 41 of 160 spectrum points are flagged.

qa.q: What would make you less sure?
qa.a: A few things would make me less sure. 41 of the 160 spectrum points are flagged. The 3.3 µm methane-band flux is faint, 0.10 ± 0.03 mJy, so the 5.1× ratio could be off by about 30%. Near 4 µm the spectrum jumps oddly, from 0.02 to 0.73 mJy. The north-south speed came out at 845 milliarcseconds per year, against 673 in the catalogue. With no Gaia match, everything rests on one published source.

qa.q: Why use both WISE and SPHEREx?
qa.a: WISE photographed this sky in 2010, and SPHEREx looked again in 2025 and 2026. Over that 16-year gap, WISE 0855-0714 moved 131 arcseconds, about 21 SPHEREx pixels. That works out to 8.27″ per year, close to the catalogue's 8.15. SPHEREx also splits light into many colors, which shows the methane dip: the object is 5.1× brighter at 4–4.75 µm than at 3.3 µm. However, 41 of its 160 spectrum points are flagged.
